domain_label: Study System — Explainability & Onboarding: Plain-Language Technical Communication
purpose: A method for turning the study app's raw internal technical state — BKT p_mastery, Elo challenge ratings, desired-retention, FK6 blueprint codes, calibration Brier/logloss, and the diagnosis 'confidence %' constant — into honest, readable, learner-facing prose across a glossary and guide page, decoding each jargon term without upgrading a heuristic constant into a probability or implying an adaptivity the app does not have.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and every reading-level or wording call is an ESTIMATE synthesized from plain-language and HCI practice, not measured on this user
the app today exposes technical state with ZERO explanation layer — no tooltips, no guide, no onboarding — so this KB writes the missing translation from scratch [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9]
the reader is a single self-studying foreign-trained dentist preparing for INBDE/TOEFL, not a machine-learning engineer, so the vocabulary ceiling is the learner's, not the model's

the tooltip-ladder UI mechanics, onboarding-flow choreography, and the visual rendering of any surface are neighboring KBs of this same uxguide specialist; this KB owns only the WORDS and their truthfulness

many decoded numbers are display-only in the shipped app (BKT/Elo/ItemElo/CalibrationBin feed no scheduling or item-selection decision), so an honest explanation must not claim they drive the plan [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.9]
exclusions: the tooltip-ladder interaction design, hover-card timing, and 'more' panel affordances (neighboring uxguide KB) beyond the reading-level discipline of what text goes in each layer
the onboarding sequencing and first-run choreography (neighboring uxguide KB) beyond the plain-language contract the onboarding copy must obey
the visual/chart rendering, color encoding and graph view (viz specialist) beyond naming what a label must say
the underlying correctness of the BKT/Elo/FSRS math itself (learner and sched specialists) — this KB explains what the numbers mean to a user, not whether the models are right
authoring the INBDE blueprint content or the FK/CC taxonomy itself (dental specialist) beyond translating its codes into a sentence a learner understands

competency_questions.question: What is the plain-language translation problem for this app, and why does it exist right now?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states that the app surfaces raw technical state (mastery, Elo, retention, FK codes, calibration, a confidence constant) with no explanation layer at all, and that the job is to translate specialists' internal reasoning into honest readable prose without lying or over-simplifying, citing APP_RECON §5.9

competency_questions.question: Who is the reader, and how does that set the vocabulary ceiling and framing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: identifies the single self-studying foreign-trained dentist (INBDE/TOEFL prep), their prior knowledge and goals, and how that bounds jargon, analogy choice and reading level

competency_questions.question: What is the honesty contract every plain-language rewrite must satisfy, and what is the canonical way it is violated?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states that a rewrite must preserve truth-value — never upgrade a heuristic constant into a probability, never imply precision or a decision that is not there — with the confidence-% constant as the flagship example

competency_questions.question: What reading-level target and concrete techniques produce readable explanations without falsifying meaning?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: gives a plain-language target (short sentences, common words, active voice, one idea per sentence, numbers in context) and the rewriting techniques that reach it, tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify

competency_questions.question: How is explanation content layered across the tooltip ladder so each layer is right-sized?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes tiny caption to hover card to 'more' panel to guide page as increasing depth, with information scent at each layer letting the reader decide whether to dig deeper, and no layer front-loading the whole story

competency_questions.question: When may an analogy be used to explain a mechanism, and how is its leakage bounded?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states analogies (e.g. Elo as a chess-style rating) aid a first grasp but leak, so each must be bounded and its break-point flagged, never left to imply properties the system lacks

competency_questions.question: Which jargon terms in this app actually need decoding, and where do they surface?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: enumerates the decode surface — FK/CC codes, BKT p_mastery, Elo challenge/elo_b, desired-retention, calibration Brier/logloss, the confidence constant, slip/guess, misconception_tag — each tied to where it appears, citing APP_RECON

competency_questions.question: How is an INBDE blueprint code like 'FK6 Pathology' explained to a learner?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: explains FK6 as one of the 10 Foundation-Knowledge areas (and CC as the clinical-content sections) used as a content axis, a hardcoded label, not the learner's score, citing APP_RECON §4c

competency_questions.question: How are the model outputs (BKT mastery, Elo challenge, calibration metrics) translated honestly, including that they are display-only?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: renders BKT p_mastery as a from-your-answers estimate (model guess, assumes no forgetting), Elo as a difficulty-match rating, calibration as prediction-vs-reality, each flagged as an estimate and as display-only where it drives no decision

competency_questions.question: How is the desired-retention slider explained so a learner sets it correctly?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: explains desired-retention (0.70–0.97) as the target share of cards you still want to remember when they come due — the single workload dial where higher means more reviews — not a report of what you have retained, citing APP_RECON §5.11

competency_questions.question: Why must the diagnosis 'confidence %' be labeled as a heuristic constant rather than a probability?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states that the rendered 'confidence 80%' is the hardcoded constant (0.4–0.8) of whichever diagnosis rule fired, not a computed posterior, and that the copy must present it honestly as a rule-strength tag, citing APP_RECON §4b

competency_questions.question: How do the glossary, guide page and a term registry work together as the reference layer?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: describes the glossary as a define-once term table, the guide page as a task-oriented layered reference, and a term-consistency registry enforcing one term one meaning across UI/glossary/guide

competency_questions.question: How are the 'why this card / why this weakness / why the plan shrank' surfaces written so they stay faithful to what the app actually does?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states each why-explanation must trace to the actual logic (e.g. the review queue is due-order first-30, not mastery-adaptive) and pass a faithfulness check against the owning specialist before shipping, citing APP_RECON §6.7/§6.9

competency_questions.question: What is the recommended plain-language stack, how is it kept in sync as the app changes, and what does it refuse to say?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: composes the go stack (audience model + honest-translation contract + reading level + layered decoding + glossary + guide + faithful why-surfaces), the maintenance-sync discipline versioning copy against the specialist logic, and the no-go on calling a constant a probability or claiming an absent decision

glossary.definition: The discipline of restating a technical internal quantity or decision in words a non-expert reader understands on first read, while preserving its exact truth-value — the core work of this KB, applied to every number and every 'why' the app surfaces.

The rule that a plain-language rewrite may simplify WORDING but never simplify MEANING: it must not upgrade a heuristic constant to a probability, imply a precision the value lacks, or claim a decision the app does not make; truthfulness outranks readability whenever they conflict.

The 'confidence 80%' shown on a diagnosed weakness — rendered as Math.round(w.confidence*100)% from WeaknessList.jsx, it is the hardcoded constant (0.4–0.8) of whichever diagnosis rule fired, NOT a computed posterior probability [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4b]; the canonical thing plain-language copy must present honestly.

INBDE blueprint axes: inbde_fk is an integer 1–10 (a 'Foundation Knowledge' area, e.g. FK6 Pathology) and inbde_cc_section is one of DTP/OHM/PP ('Clinical Content' sections); they are hardcoded content labels the app aggregates mastery onto, not the learner's score [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c].

The learner-model estimate, per concept, of the probability the learner knows that concept, inferred from their answer stream by Bayesian Knowledge Tracing; a model guess that assumes no forgetting and, as shipped, is display-only (feeds no scheduling) [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.9].

A chess-style rating that scores learner ability per concept and difficulty per card so questions can be matched to level; in this app the item difficulty elo_b is computed but rendered by no page and used by no selector [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c/§6.9].

The Settings slider (0.70–0.97) setting the target share of cards you still want to be able to recall when they fall due — the single FSRS workload dial, where a higher target schedules more reviews; it is a target you choose, not a report of what you have already retained [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.11].

Per-run measures of how close the app's recall predictions were to what actually happened (lower is better), written to CalibrationBin/SystemMetrics; internal quality metrics currently rendered by no page [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c/§3].

Layering explanation by depth — a tiny caption, then a hover card, then a 'more' panel, then the guide page — so a reader gets a one-line answer in place and can descend for detail only if they want it; this KB governs the words at each layer, not the interaction mechanics.

The verification that a user-facing explanation matches what the app actually does before it ships — e.g. that a 'why this card' line does not claim adaptive selection when the queue is due-order first-30 — cross-checked against the owning specialist and the code behavior [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.7].

nodes.definition: Frame the problem: the study app surfaces raw internal technical state — BKT p_mastery, Elo challenge ratings, desired-retention, FK/CC blueprint codes, calibration Brier/logloss, and a diagnosis 'confidence %' — with ZERO explanation layer (no tooltips, no guide, no onboarding) [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9]. The job of this KB is to translate the specialists' internal reasoning and outputs into honest, readable, learner-facing prose: not to dumb it down until it is false, and not to leave it in engineer's vocabulary. Plain-language technical communication sits between the specialists (who own the truth of each number) and the reader (who owns the vocabulary), producing the words that go into every caption, tooltip, glossary entry, guide section and 'why' surface [ESTIMATE — design synthesis over the app recon].

excluded: the correctness of the underlying models (learner/sched specialists)

pros.claim: Naming the mission as truth-preserving translation, not decoration, keeps every later wording choice accountable to meaning
pros.example: treating a tooltip for 'confidence 80%' as an honesty obligation rather than a nicety

cons.claim: Because no explanation layer exists yet, every surface must be written from scratch with no prior copy to lean on
cons.example: having to invent the first honest sentence for BKT mastery with no house style to inherit

failure_modes: treating explanation copy as cosmetic polish rather than a truth obligation
leaving engineer vocabulary in the UI because 'it is technically correct'
acceptance_tests: the frame states the zero-explanation starting condition with the APP_RECON §5.9 citation, the honest-translation mission, and the intermediary position between specialists and reader
revisit_triggers: the app adds a native help or onboarding layer
a specialist changes what internal state is surfaced to the user
a new jargon surface appears in the UI

base.update_signal: a native help layer or a new surfaced quantity changes the framing

nodes.definition: Fix who the reader is, because it sets the vocabulary ceiling, the framing and the analogy palette. The reader is a single self-studying learner — a foreign-trained dentist preparing for INBDE and TOEFL — motivated and domain-literate in dentistry but NOT a machine-learning engineer: 'pathology' is familiar, 'Bayesian posterior' and 'logloss' are not [ESTIMATE — inferred from the app's stated user in APP_RECON/SPECIALIST_LIST]. Explanations therefore lean on the learner's clinical and test-prep mental model, spend the jargon budget on exam terms the reader already owns, and translate every ML/statistics term. The reader's goal is to pass, so copy is framed around 'what should I do / what does this mean for my studying', not around model internals for their own sake.

excluded: persona research or multi-user segmentation (single-user app)
the specific reading-level metric (its own node)

pros.claim: A concrete reader model tells you which words are free (clinical/exam terms) and which must be translated (ML/stats terms)
pros.example: leaving 'pathology' untranslated while rewriting 'Bayesian mastery estimate' into 'our guess of how well you know this'

cons.claim: Assuming one reader profile risks copy that misfits a learner with more or less statistical background than modeled
cons.example: over-explaining probability to a reader who happens to have a quantitative degree

failure_modes: writing for an imagined ML-literate user and leaving stats jargon in place
stripping clinical terms the reader actually knows and sounding condescending
acceptance_tests: the reader is identified as the single foreign-trained-dentist INBDE/TOEFL learner, and the clinical-literate-not-ML-literate ceiling and action-framed stance are stated
revisit_triggers: the app targets a broader or different user
reader confusion clusters on a term assumed familiar
the exam scope changes the domain vocabulary

base.update_signal: a change of target user or recurring confusion on an assumed-familiar term revises the reader model

nodes.definition: State the non-negotiable contract: a plain-language rewrite may simplify WORDING but must never simplify MEANING. Concretely it must not (a) upgrade a heuristic constant into a probability, (b) imply a precision the value does not have, (c) claim a decision or adaptivity the app does not actually perform, or (d) present an estimate as a fact. Where readability and truth conflict, truth wins and the copy stays a little longer or hedged rather than becoming false [FACT for this design rule as authored here; the honesty obligation is this KB's own contract]. The flagship case is the rendered 'confidence 80%', a hardcoded rule constant that dishonest copy would call a probability. This contract is the acceptance criterion every other node's output is checked against.

included: the four forbidden distortions (constant-as-probability, false precision, phantom decision, estimate-as-fact)
excluded: the specific decode of each term (their own nodes)
the reading-level techniques that do the simplifying

pros.claim: A single explicit contract gives every explanation a pass/fail check independent of who wrote it
pros.example: rejecting a tooltip that says 'we are 80% sure' because the 80% is a fixed rule constant

cons.claim: Holding truth above readability sometimes forces a hedged, slightly longer sentence that a marketer would cut
cons.example: keeping 'this is our estimate, not a measurement' where a punchier line would drop the caveat

failure_modes: dropping a caveat to make a line snappier and thereby implying certainty
letting a plausible-sounding simplification quietly change what is claimed
acceptance_tests: the contract states simplify-wording-not-meaning, lists the forbidden distortions with the confidence-constant example, and makes truth outrank readability on conflict
revisit_triggers: a shipped explanation is found to overstate certainty or a decision
a new class of value (e.g. a new score) needs an honesty rule
the underlying quantity changes from constant to computed or vice versa

base.update_signal: an overstated shipped explanation or a new value class changes the contract

nodes.definition: Set the readability target: short sentences (roughly one clause each), common words over technical synonyms, active voice, one idea per sentence, and every number given in context rather than bare [ESTIMATE — standard plain-language guidance, to source-verify against a named style guide]. The aim is that the reader understands the sentence on first read without re-parsing, at a reading level well below the density of the source specialists' prose. Crucially the target constrains FORM, not TRUTH: it is the readability half of the honest-translation contract, and it may never be reached by deleting a caveat the contract requires. A concrete self-check is reading the sentence aloud once and asking whether a tired learner would get it.

excluded: any claim that simplicity can override the honesty contract

pros.claim: A concrete readability target makes 'plain enough' checkable instead of a matter of taste
pros.example: flagging a 40-word passive sentence with three clauses for a rewrite before it ships

cons.claim: Reading-level targets are heuristics not laws, and a mechanical grade score can be gamed while meaning stays murky
cons.example: hitting a grade metric by chopping sentences while leaving an undefined term in place

failure_modes: chasing a grade-level number while comprehension actually drops
reaching the target by cutting a required caveat
acceptance_tests: the target names short sentences, common words, active voice, one-idea-per-sentence and numbers-in-context, tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify, and subordinates readability to the honesty contract
revisit_triggers: a named plain-language standard is adopted to source-verify against
readers still misread copy that meets the target
the target is being gamed without comprehension gains

base.update_signal: adopting a named standard or persistent misreads changes the target

nodes.definition: Enumerate the moves that reach the readability target without falsifying meaning: replace or gloss each jargon term on first use; define-once and reuse; prefer a concrete example or a bounded analogy to an abstract definition; turn nominalizations back into verbs ('calibration of predictions' becomes 'checking whether our guesses came true'); give a number a referent and direction ('0.72' becomes 'about 7 in 10, and higher is better'); and lead with the reader's takeaway before the mechanism [ESTIMATE — plain-language and technical-communication practice, to source-verify]. Each technique is a wording change only; none may drop a caveat the honesty contract requires, and any analogy must obey the analogy-discipline node.

pros.claim: A named technique set turns 'make it clearer' into specific repeatable edits
pros.example: rewriting 'logloss decreased' as 'our recall predictions got closer to what actually happened'

cons.claim: Applied mechanically the moves can over-simplify and strip nuance the value carries
cons.example: reducing 'estimate that assumes no forgetting' to a flat 'how well you know it' and losing the caveat

failure_modes: over-simplifying until a required nuance is gone
using an analogy that leaks without bounding it
acceptance_tests: the node lists the rewriting moves (gloss, define-once, example/analogy, de-nominalize, number-with-referent, takeaway-first) and requires each to keep the contract's caveats
revisit_triggers: a technique is found to routinely strip a needed caveat
a new content type needs a new move
source-verification revises the recommended techniques

base.update_signal: a caveat-stripping pattern or a new content type changes the technique set

nodes.definition: Govern how much explanation goes in each rung of the tooltip ladder: a tiny in-place caption gives the one-line meaning; a hover card adds the key caveat and a 'why it matters'; a 'more' panel adds the mechanism and edge cases; the guide page holds the full treatment [ESTIMATE — progressive-disclosure practice, to source-verify]. Each layer must be complete-enough to stand alone at its depth and must not front-load a deeper layer's detail. This KB owns the WORDING budget per layer (how much truth fits in a caption vs a panel), not the interaction mechanics, which are a neighboring uxguide KB. The honest-translation contract holds at every layer: a caption may be short but never false.

included: each layer stands alone and does not front-load
excluded: hover timing and interaction mechanics (neighboring KB)
the guide page's internal structure (own node)

pros.claim: Layering lets a caption stay short and honest while depth waits one click away for the reader who wants it
pros.example: a caption 'estimated mastery' expanding on hover to 'our guess from your answers; it assumes you do not forget'

cons.claim: Splitting a truth across layers risks a caption that is honest but too thin to prevent a misread before the reader hovers
cons.example: 'confidence 80%' as a bare caption misread as a probability by a reader who never opens the deeper layer

failure_modes: cramming the full explanation into a caption
leaving a caption so thin it invites the very misread the deeper layer prevents
acceptance_tests: the ladder assigns caption/hover/more/guide by depth, requires each layer to stand alone without front-loading, and holds the honesty contract at every layer
revisit_triggers: a caption is misread before its deeper layer is opened
the ladder's rungs change in the UI
a value needs its caveat promoted to a shallower layer

base.update_signal: a pre-hover misread or a ladder change revises the layering

nodes.definition: Label surfaces so a reader can tell what lies deeper and decide whether to dig, giving every jargon token a visible 'what is this?' affordance rather than leaving a bare number unexplained [ESTIMATE — information-scent / findability practice, to source-verify]. Good scent means the caption or icon truthfully previews the deeper content so the reader's click is rewarded, not baited; the label must match what the next layer actually says. In this app that means an explain-affordance on FK codes, mastery bars, Elo figures, retention slider and the confidence tag — the exact surfaces that today carry no hover hint at all [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.9]. Weak or misleading scent (a label that oversells the depth behind it) is itself a small honesty violation.

included: the explain-affordance on every jargon token
truthful preview so clicks are rewarded not baited
excluded: the deeper layer's full copy (layering node)

pros.claim: Consistent explain-affordances let a curious reader self-serve and a hurried one ignore detail without being blocked
pros.example: a small '?' on the retention slider that previews 'what target retention does' before the reader commits to reading

cons.claim: Affordances everywhere can clutter and, if the preview oversells, erode trust when the depth disappoints
cons.example: a '?' promising an explanation that only restates the label the reader already didn't understand

failure_modes: leaving a jargon number with no explain-affordance at all
a scent label that oversells or misdescribes the deeper content
acceptance_tests: the node requires an explain-affordance on each jargon surface, requires the preview to match the deeper content, and cites the current no-hint state (APP_RECON §5.9)
revisit_triggers: readers miss an explanation because a surface had no affordance
an affordance's preview is found to oversell its depth
a new jargon surface ships without a hint

base.update_signal: a missed-explanation surface or an overselling preview changes the scent rules

nodes.definition: Rule the use of analogies, which are the strongest first-grasp tool and the easiest way to lie by accident. An analogy (Elo as a chess-style rating, desired-retention as a thermostat, mastery as a fuel gauge) may be used to seed intuition, but every analogy leaks: the reader can import properties the system lacks. Discipline: pick an analogy that matches on the ONE property being taught, state what it teaches, and flag where it breaks before the reader over-extends it [ESTIMATE — technical-communication practice, to source-verify]. An unbounded analogy violates the honesty contract as surely as a false number — e.g. 'chess rating' wrongly implying the learner competes against or 'loses points to' a card. When no honest bounded analogy exists, prefer a plain example.

included: fall back to a plain example when no honest analogy fits
excluded: the specific decode copy per term (decode nodes)

pros.claim: A bounded analogy gives instant intuition for an abstract mechanism at almost no reading cost
pros.example: 'target retention is like a thermostat: set it higher and the app schedules more reviews to hold that level'

cons.claim: Every analogy leaks, and a reader who over-extends it can end up more wrong than with no analogy
cons.example: 'chess rating' leading a learner to think a wrong answer means they 'lost to' the card

failure_modes: using an analogy without stating where it breaks
picking an analogy that matches on a property other than the one being taught
acceptance_tests: the node requires one-property-match selection, an explicit teaches/breaks statement per analogy, and a plain-example fallback, tagged ESTIMATE to source-verify
revisit_triggers: a shipped analogy is found to mislead
a clearer bounded analogy is discovered for a term
a term proves to have no honest analogy

base.update_signal: a misleading shipped analogy or a better bounded analogy changes the rule

nodes.definition: Enumerate the decode surface — the specific technical tokens the app shows a learner that need translation, each tied to where it appears: FK/CC blueprint codes (LearnerModel/MasteryTrendChart labels), BKT p_mastery and the MasteryBars color bands, Elo challenge / elo_b item difficulty, desired-retention slider (Settings), calibration Brier/logloss and CalibrationBin, the diagnosis 'confidence %' on WeaknessList, and the diagnosis vocabulary itself (slip, misconception, missing_prereq, retrieval_decay, misconception_tag) [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4b/§4c/§5.11]. This inventory is the worklist the glossary and tooltips must cover; a token in the UI with no entry is an unmet obligation. It is deliberately scoped to what the app SHOWS, not every internal field, so effort tracks reader-visible confusion.

included: the reader-visible token list (FK/CC, mastery, Elo, retention, calibration, confidence, diagnosis terms)
each token tied to its UI location
scope limited to what the app shows
excluded: internal-only fields never shown to the reader

pros.claim: A concrete inventory makes coverage checkable — every visible token maps to a planned explanation
pros.example: confirming the retention slider, mastery bars and confidence tag each have a glossary entry queued

cons.claim: The UI changes, so an inventory pinned to today's surfaces goes stale as screens are added or removed
cons.example: a new chart shipping an untranslated metric the inventory never listed

failure_modes: missing a visible token so it ships unexplained
padding the inventory with internal fields the reader never sees
acceptance_tests: the inventory lists the reader-visible tokens with their UI locations citing APP_RECON, and scopes itself to what the app shows
revisit_triggers: a new UI surface exposes a new token
a token is removed from the UI
readers report confusion on a token not in the inventory

base.update_signal: a new or removed UI token changes the inventory

nodes.definition: Translate the INBDE blueprint codes. 'FK6 Pathology' is one of the 10 Foundation-Knowledge areas (inbde_fk, an integer 1–10), and DTP/OHM/PP are the three Clinical-Content sections (inbde_cc_section); the app aggregates mastery onto these axes for its remediation report, and the display names are hardcoded labels [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c]. The learner-facing line makes clear this is a CONTENT category on the exam blueprint — 'the exam groups topics into 10 knowledge areas; FK6 is Pathology' — and explicitly NOT the learner's score or a difficulty. The reader already owns 'pathology', so the translation spends its words on 'what FK6 means as a grouping', not on defining pathology.

excluded: the mastery number aggregated onto the axis (mastery decode node)

pros.claim: Framing FK/CC as blueprint content areas stops a learner reading 'FK6' as a grade or a difficulty rank
pros.example: 'FK6 Pathology is one of ten exam knowledge areas; this bar shows your average mastery within it'

cons.claim: The codes are exam-org jargon whose meaning depends on the blueprint, so the copy leans on the dental specialist staying current
cons.example: a blueprint revision renaming an FK area while the tooltip still shows the old label

failure_modes: letting a learner read FK6 as their score or a difficulty level
over-defining familiar clinical terms instead of the grouping
acceptance_tests: the decode states FK as the 10 Foundation-Knowledge areas and CC as the DTP/OHM/PP sections, frames them as content axes not scores, and cites APP_RECON §4c
revisit_triggers: the INBDE blueprint labels change
a learner misreads an FK/CC code as a score
the finer inbde_cc 1–56 field becomes surfaced

base.update_signal: a blueprint relabel or a surfaced finer code changes the decode

nodes.definition: Translate BKT p_mastery honestly: it is the app's ESTIMATE, per concept, of how well the learner knows that concept, inferred from their answer history — 'our best guess from your answers', not a measurement and not a certainty. The honest caveats the copy must carry: it is a model estimate that can be wrong, it assumes the learner does not forget (so it only rises with practice and does not by itself say a concept is due), and as shipped it is DISPLAY-ONLY — nothing reads it to schedule or pick cards [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.9]. The MasteryBars color bands (green ≥60%, yellow ≥40%, else red) get a one-line legend, and the number is given with direction ('higher means our estimate says you know it better'). The word chosen for it must be used consistently everywhere (term registry).

included: p_mastery as a from-answers estimate not a measurement

pros.claim: Calling mastery an estimate with a no-forgetting caveat stops a learner treating a green bar as proof they are done
pros.example: 'estimated mastery 72% — our guess from your answers; it does not account for forgetting'

cons.claim: The honest caveats make the number sound softer, which can frustrate a learner who wanted a hard verdict
cons.example: a reader annoyed that the app 'won't just tell me if I know it' once the estimate is hedged

failure_modes: presenting the estimate as a measured fact
implying a high bar means the card is handled when scheduling is separate
acceptance_tests: the decode renders p_mastery as a from-answers estimate, carries the no-forgetting and display-only caveats citing APP_RECON §6.9, and legends the MasteryBars bands
revisit_triggers: mastery starts driving a real decision (no longer display-only)
the color bands change
a learner reads the estimate as a measurement

base.update_signal: mastery becoming decision-driving or a band change updates the decode

nodes.definition: Translate the Elo challenge calibration: a chess-style rating that scores the learner's level per concept and each card's difficulty (elo_b), so questions could be matched to the right challenge. The honest copy uses a BOUNDED chess-rating analogy (see analogy discipline) — 'like a chess rating for you and for each card' — and immediately bounds it: the learner is not competing, and a wrong answer is not 'losing'. It must also state that in the shipped app the item difficulty is computed but DISPLAY-ONLY: rendered by no page and used by no selector, so it does not currently change which cards appear [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c/§6.9]. Because BKT mastery and Elo both sound like 'how well you know it', the copy must distinguish their jobs to avoid a two-numbers confusion.

included: Elo as a bounded chess-style rating of learner and card

pros.claim: A bounded rating analogy gives instant intuition for difficulty-matching while the bound blocks the 'losing points' misread
pros.example: 'each card has a difficulty rating; when yours is close, the card is well-matched — you are not playing against it'

cons.claim: Explaining a display-only rating risks implying the app already adapts card choice when it does not
cons.example: 'matched to your level' read as a live adaptive queue that the shipped app lacks

failure_modes: letting the chess analogy imply competition or point-loss
implying Elo already drives card selection when it is display-only
acceptance_tests: the decode uses a bounded chess-rating analogy with its break-point flagged, states elo_b is display-only citing APP_RECON, and separates Elo's job from mastery's
revisit_triggers: Elo begins driving card selection

nodes.definition: Translate the desired-retention slider (0.70–0.97): it sets the TARGET share of cards you still want to be able to recall when they come due — the single workload dial, where setting it higher schedules more reviews to hold that higher target [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.11]. The critical honesty point is that it is a target the learner CHOOSES, not a report of what they have already retained: 'desired retention 0.90 means you are aiming to remember 9 in 10 cards at review time', with a plain trade-off line ('higher = better recall but more daily reviews'). A bounded thermostat analogy is allowed. The copy must not let the learner read it as a current-performance readout, which would invert its meaning.

included: retention as a chosen target share of recall at due-time
excluded: the calibration metrics that measure realized recall (own node)

pros.claim: Framing retention as a chosen target with a workload trade-off lets a learner set it deliberately instead of guessing
pros.example: 'aim to remember 9 in 10 (0.90); raise it for safer recall and more reviews, lower it for less load'

cons.claim: A one-line trade-off understates the real load curve, so a learner may set an unsustainable target
cons.example: a learner picking 0.97 without grasping how many extra daily reviews it implies

failure_modes: letting the learner read it as how much they have retained rather than a target
hiding the workload cost of a high target
acceptance_tests: the decode states retention is a chosen target share of recall at due-time with the higher-more-reviews trade-off, warns it is not a current-performance readout, and cites APP_RECON §5.11
revisit_triggers: the slider range or its role changes
learners set unsustainable targets
a live workload preview is added

base.update_signal: a slider-role change or unsustainable-target reports update the decode

nodes.definition: Handle the flagship honesty case. The weakness list renders 'confidence 80%' as Math.round(w.confidence*100)% from WeaknessList.jsx, and that value is the HARDCODED constant (between 0.4 and 0.8) attached to whichever diagnosis rule fired — NOT a computed posterior probability [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4b]. Plain-language copy must therefore present it as a rule-strength tag, not a probability: honest phrasing is 'how strongly this rule matched' or 'diagnosis strength', explicitly avoiding 'we are 80% sure' or any 'probability' wording. The decode names the five rules' fixed levels (misconception 0.8, missing_prereq/retrieval_decay 0.7, slip 0.6, under-sampled fallback 0.4) as preset labels for match strength, so the learner reads a categorical confidence tag, not a calibrated chance. This node is the concrete embodiment of the honest-translation contract.

included: confidence-% as a hardcoded per-rule constant
rule-strength / diagnosis-strength phrasing, never 'probability' or 'X% sure'
the five fixed rule levels as preset labels
excluded: the diagnosis rules' clinical logic (learner specialist)

pros.claim: Presenting the number as a rule-strength tag prevents the single most damaging honesty error — a constant read as a calibrated probability
pros.example: 'diagnosis strength: high' or 'this rule matched strongly' instead of 'we are 80% sure'

cons.claim: A learner used to percentages may find a strength label vaguer and want the number back
cons.example: a reader asking 'but what are the actual odds' when the honest answer is that there are none computed

failure_modes: writing 'we are 80% sure' or 'probability' for a hardcoded constant
implying the five levels are calibrated chances rather than preset tags
acceptance_tests: the decode states the confidence % is a hardcoded per-rule constant citing APP_RECON §4b, prescribes rule-strength phrasing and bans probability wording, and lists the five fixed levels as preset labels
revisit_triggers: the diagnosis confidence becomes an actual computed probability
the rule set or its constants change
a shipped surface calls the constant a probability

base.update_signal: the confidence becoming computed or a probability-mislabel shipping changes the decode

nodes.definition: Translate the calibration metrics IF and WHERE they are ever surfaced: Brier and logloss (in CalibrationBin and SystemMetrics) measure how close the app's recall predictions were to what actually happened, with lower being better [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c/§3]. The honest plain-language line is 'how well our recall guesses matched reality — lower means our guesses were closer', never the raw statistic name unglossed. The important honesty note is that these are INTERNAL quality metrics rendered by no page today [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4c], so unless a surface is added the default is to NOT expose them to the learner at all; over-explaining an internal metric adds noise. When surfaced (e.g. a 'how accurate are our predictions' panel), the copy gives direction and a plain referent, not the number alone.

included: the default of not surfacing an internal metric
excluded: the mastery and Elo decodes (own nodes)

pros.claim: A plain gloss lets a curious learner understand prediction accuracy without the raw statistic, while defaulting to hide it avoids clutter
pros.example: 'our recall predictions matched reality well this week' rather than exposing a bare Brier score

cons.claim: Deciding what stays internal is a judgment call, and hiding a metric can look opaque if a learner glimpses it elsewhere
cons.example: a metric visible in an export but with no in-app explanation because it was deemed internal

failure_modes: exposing a raw Brier/logloss number with no gloss
over-surfacing an internal metric the learner does not need
acceptance_tests: the decode glosses Brier/logloss as prediction-vs-reality closeness (lower better), notes they are internal and unrendered by default citing APP_RECON §4c, and requires direction-and-referent phrasing if surfaced
revisit_triggers: a page begins rendering calibration to the learner
a learner encounters the metric with no explanation
the metric set changes

base.update_signal: calibration being surfaced to the learner changes the decode

nodes.definition: Define the glossary as the single define-once source of truth: a term-to-plain-definition table covering every token in the jargon inventory, each entry carrying the honest caveats its decode node prescribes, written at the reading-level target. The glossary is what the tooltip 'more' layer and the guide page LINK to rather than re-writing, so a definition is authored once and reused everywhere — the mechanism that makes term consistency enforceable [ESTIMATE — reference-artifact design practice]. Each entry states what the term means, gives a referent/direction for any number, and flags estimate-vs-fact and display-only status where relevant. An inventory token with no glossary entry is an open gap; a glossary entry no UI token uses is dead weight to prune.

included: the define-once term table covering the inventory
carrying each decode's caveats at the reading-level target
link-not-rewrite reuse by tooltips and guide
excluded: the guide page's task structure (own node)

pros.claim: One authored definition per term, linked everywhere, kills drift and makes coverage auditable against the inventory
pros.example: the mastery definition written once and surfaced identically in the tooltip and the guide

cons.claim: A central glossary can lag the UI if new tokens are not added, leaving fresh surfaces linking to nothing
cons.example: a new metric shipping with a tooltip that links to a missing glossary entry

failure_modes: a UI token with no glossary entry
re-writing a definition inline instead of linking, reintroducing drift
acceptance_tests: the glossary is specified as a define-once table covering the inventory, carrying decode caveats at the reading-level target, and linked (not rewritten) by tooltips and the guide
revisit_triggers: the jargon inventory gains or loses a token
a definition is found re-written inline somewhere
a decode node's caveats change

base.update_signal: an inventory change or an inline-rewritten definition changes the glossary

nodes.definition: Structure the guide page as the deepest, standalone layer: task-oriented sections answering the learner's real questions ('how does the app decide what to review', 'what do the mastery colors mean', 'how is a weakness diagnosed', 'how do I set retention') rather than a data dictionary. It links terms to the glossary instead of redefining them, orders sections by reader need, and keeps each section at the reading-level target with the honest caveats intact [ESTIMATE — help-system and minimalist-documentation practice, to source-verify]. It is the honest full-treatment layer the tooltip ladder descends to. Because it explains how the app behaves, every behavioral claim in it is subject to the faithfulness check — the guide must describe what the app actually does, including where a feature is display-only.

included: task-oriented how-does-X sections ordered by reader need
linking terms to the glossary not redefining
behavioral claims subject to the faithfulness check
excluded: the visual layout/rendering of the page (viz specialist)

pros.claim: A task-oriented guide answers the questions a learner actually asks, not a term list they must assemble themselves
pros.example: a 'how the app picks today's cards' section instead of scattered field definitions

cons.claim: A behavioral guide goes stale the moment the app's behavior changes, and stale how-it-works copy is worse than none
cons.example: a guide still describing due-order review after an adaptive queue ships, or vice versa

failure_modes: writing a data-dictionary instead of task-oriented answers
making a behavioral claim the app does not honor
acceptance_tests: the guide is specified as task-oriented sections ordered by reader need, links terms to the glossary, and subjects every behavioral claim to the faithfulness check
revisit_triggers: app behavior described in the guide changes
a section proves to answer no real reader question
a behavioral claim fails the faithfulness check

base.update_signal: an app-behavior change or a failed faithfulness claim changes the guide

nodes.definition: Write the 'why' surfaces — 'why this card now', 'why this weakness was diagnosed', 'why the plan shrank' — as short honest explanations of the actual mechanism. Each must trace to real logic: 'why this weakness' cites the diagnosis rule that fired and its rule-strength tag (not a probability); 'why the plan shrank' cites the heuristic feasibility simulation and the workload/retention inputs; and 'why this card now' must NOT claim adaptive or mastery-based selection, because the shipped review queue takes the first 30 due cards in due order with no mastery or Elo input [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.7/§6.9]. The discipline is: explain the cause that actually operates, in the learner's language, and where the honest cause is dull ('it was simply due next') say that rather than inventing a smarter-sounding reason.

included: why-weakness citing the fired rule and its strength tag
why-plan citing the feasibility simulation and inputs

pros.claim: Honest why-lines build trust and teach the learner how the app really works, even when the real reason is mundane
pros.example: 'this card is up because it was next in your due queue' rather than implying a clever choice

cons.claim: The true reason is sometimes unimpressive, tempting copy that sounds smarter than the system is
cons.example: dressing up due-order selection as 'chosen to match your level' when nothing does that

failure_modes: inventing an adaptive-sounding reason the app does not implement
citing the confidence constant as a probability in a why-weakness line
acceptance_tests: the why-surfaces trace to the actual mechanism, state due-order (not adaptivity) for why-this-card citing APP_RECON §6.7/§6.9, and use rule-strength not probability for why-weakness
revisit_triggers: the selection, diagnosis or planning logic changes
a why-surface is found to overstate the mechanism
a new why-surface is added

base.update_signal: a change in selection/diagnosis/planning logic or an overstated why-line changes the prose

nodes.definition: Define the verification that every user-facing explanation matches what the app actually does before it ships. A plain-language claim the system does not honor is a lie, however readable — so each behavioral statement (in a why-surface, a decode caveat, or the guide) is cross-checked against the actual code behavior and confirmed with the owning specialist [FACT for this check as this KB's discipline; the canonical failure is claiming adaptivity where the queue is due-order first-30, APP_RECON §6.7]. The check specifically catches: claiming a display-only number drives a decision, calling a heuristic constant a probability, and describing an unshipped or phantom feature as live. It is the gate between drafted copy and published copy, and it is re-run whenever the underlying behavior changes.

included: cross-checking every behavioral claim against actual code and the owning specialist
catching phantom-decision, constant-as-probability and unshipped-feature claims

pros.claim: A ship gate against actual behavior stops readable-but-false copy from reaching the learner
pros.example: blocking a 'matched to your level' tooltip once the check confirms selection is due-order only

cons.claim: The check costs a cross-reference with the owning specialist and can bottleneck fast copy changes
cons.example: a wording tweak waiting on confirmation of exactly what the scheduler does

failure_modes: shipping a behavioral claim without verifying it against the code
verifying once and never re-checking after the behavior changes
acceptance_tests: the check cross-verifies every behavioral claim against code and the owning specialist, catches phantom-decision/constant-as-probability/unshipped-feature errors, and gates draft-to-publish citing APP_RECON §6.7
revisit_triggers: a shipped explanation is found unfaithful
the underlying app behavior changes
a new behavioral surface is added

base.update_signal: an unfaithful shipped explanation or an app-behavior change re-runs the check

nodes.definition: Enforce one term, one meaning across the UI, glossary and guide: pick a single learner-facing word for each concept (e.g. settle on 'mastery' and never drift to 'knowledge', 'proficiency' or 'skill level' for the same number) and record the chosen term and its banned synonyms in a small registry the glossary anchors [ESTIMATE — controlled-vocabulary / terminology-management practice]. Inconsistent naming makes a learner think two labels are two things. The registry also fixes the honest framing word per value — 'estimated', 'target', 'rule-strength' — so the caveat travels with the term wherever it is used. New copy must draw its nouns from the registry, and any needed new term is added there first.

included: one chosen learner-facing term per concept with banned synonyms
fixing the honest framing word per value
new copy drawing nouns from the registry

pros.claim: A term registry stops synonym drift that makes one number look like several different things
pros.example: always saying 'estimated mastery' so the learner never wonders how it differs from 'proficiency'

cons.claim: Rigid terminology can force a slightly awkward word where a context-specific synonym would read better
cons.example: keeping 'mastery' in a sentence where 'how well you know it' would flow more naturally

failure_modes: letting two synonyms name the same value across surfaces
coining a new term in copy without registering it
acceptance_tests: the registry fixes one learner-facing term per concept with banned synonyms and the honest framing word per value, and requires new copy to draw from it
revisit_triggers: a synonym for a registered term appears in shipped copy
a new concept needs a registered term
a chosen term proves to confuse readers

base.update_signal: a synonym drift or a new concept term changes the registry

nodes.definition: Keep the explanation layer in sync with the logic it describes: because the app's behavior and the specialists' models evolve, the glossary, guide, decodes and why-surfaces must be versioned against the specialist logic they explain, so a change in behavior triggers a copy review [ESTIMATE — documentation-maintenance practice]. The specific drift risks in this app are concrete: BKT parameters are never re-fit and Elo uncertainty decays to a floor no matter the outcome, so 'confidence'-flavored copy can grow stale; features described as display-only may become decision-driving; and diagnosis constants could change [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.4]. The discipline pairs each behavioral explanation with a pointer to the code/specialist it depends on, and re-runs the faithfulness check when that dependency changes.

included: versioning copy against the specialist logic it explains
pairing each behavioral explanation with its code/specialist dependency
re-running the faithfulness check on dependency change
excluded: the one-time faithfulness check itself (own node)

pros.claim: Tying each explanation to its logic dependency turns silent drift into a triggered review
pros.example: flagging the mastery copy for review when the learner specialist changes how mastery is computed

cons.claim: Maintaining dependency links is overhead that decays if no one keeps the pointers current
cons.example: a copy-to-code pointer going stale so a behavior change never triggers the intended review

failure_modes: copy silently describing an old behavior after the logic changed
dependency pointers rotting so change triggers no review
acceptance_tests: the discipline versions copy against specialist logic, pairs each behavioral explanation with its dependency citing APP_RECON §6.4, and re-runs the faithfulness check on change
revisit_triggers: a specialist changes a described behavior
a display-only feature becomes decision-driving
a dependency pointer is found stale

base.update_signal: a described-behavior change or a stale dependency pointer triggers a copy review

nodes.definition: Compose the recommended plain-language stack this KB builds toward. Go: model the single INBDE/TOEFL reader; hold every rewrite to the honest-translation contract; hit the reading-level target with the named techniques and bounded analogies; layer content down the tooltip ladder with truthful information scent; decode each visible token (FK/CC, mastery, Elo, retention, calibration) with its caveats and its display-only status; centralize in a define-once glossary and a task-oriented guide governed by a term registry; write faithful why-surfaces; and version it all against the specialist logic. No-go, the explicit refusals: never call the diagnosis 'confidence %' a probability (it is a hardcoded rule constant [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4b]), never claim a decision the app does not make (the review queue is due-order, not adaptive [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.7]), and never simplify wording at the cost of meaning. An explanation earns a place only when it is readable, honest, faithful to actual behavior, and kept in sync.

included: the go stack (reader model + contract + reading level + layering + decodes + glossary/guide/registry + faithful why-surfaces + maintenance sync)
the no-go on constant-as-probability, phantom-decision and meaning-losing simplification
excluded: the neighboring uxguide tooltip-mechanics and onboarding KBs
the other specialists' model and rendering decisions

pros.claim: The merged verdict commits to a readable AND honest explanation layer and names exactly what it refuses to say
pros.example: shipping decoded tooltips and a guide while banning 'we are 80% sure' and 'matched to your level' copy

cons.claim: A strict honesty-first stack produces softer, more caveated copy than a marketing voice would, and defers polish to keep truth
cons.example: a hedged mastery tooltip that a growth team would rewrite punchier and less accurately

failure_modes: shipping copy that trades truth for punch against the no-go
adopting an explanation that is not faithful to actual behavior or not kept in sync
acceptance_tests: the verdict states the go stack, the no-go on constant-as-probability (APP_RECON §4b) and phantom-decision (APP_RECON §6.7) and meaning-losing simplification, and the readable/honest/faithful/in-sync acceptance rule
revisit_triggers: a described behavior changes and cascades through the stack
a shipped surface violates a no-go
the reader model or exposed token set changes materially

base.update_signal: a behavior change, a no-go violation, or a reader/token-set change revises the verdict

conflict_axes.name: simplicity_vs_truth

conflict_axes.resolution_hint: simplify wording, never meaning; truth outranks readability and a required caveat stays even if the sentence grows

conflict_axes.name: analogy_clarity_vs_leakage
conflict_axes.description: The analogy that best seeds intuition usually imports properties the system does not have.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use only bounded analogies — one matched property, teaches-and-breaks stated — else a plain example

conflict_axes.name: in_context_brevity_vs_comprehensive_guide

conflict_axes.name: show_confidence_vs_admit_heuristic

workflow.gate: the glossary covers the inventory, the guide is task-oriented and links terms, and the registry fixes one term per concept

workflow.action: Write the why-surfaces and run the faithfulness check
workflow.description: Draft why-this-card/weakness/plan lines and cross-check every behavioral claim against actual code and the owning specialist
workflow.gate: why-this-card states due-order not adaptivity (APP_RECON §6.7) and every behavioral claim passes the check before publish

workflow.action: Version copy against logic and issue the verdict
workflow.description: Pair each behavioral explanation with its dependency and commit to the go stack with its explicit no-goes
workflow.gate: the go stack and the no-go on constant-as-probability, phantom-decision and meaning-losing simplification are stated with the readable/honest/faithful/in-sync rule

dominance_rules.rule: Truth dominates readability whenever they conflict
dominance_rules.rationale: a readable-but-false explanation is worse than a slightly longer honest one, and this is the whole point of technical communication here
dominance_rules.trigger: a simplification would drop a required caveat or imply certainty
dominance_rules.action: keep the caveat and simplify only wording, accepting a longer or hedged sentence

dominance_rules.rule: A rule-strength framing dominates any probability wording for the confidence constant
dominance_rules.rationale: the 'confidence %' is a hardcoded per-rule constant, not a computed posterior [FACT-source: APP_RECON §4b]
dominance_rules.trigger: the diagnosis confidence value is about to be shown or captioned
dominance_rules.action: present it as diagnosis/rule strength and ban 'probability' and 'X% sure' phrasing

dominance_rules.rule: The actual mechanism dominates the impressive-sounding one in every why-surface
dominance_rules.rationale: the shipped review queue is due-order first-30 with no adaptivity, so any smarter narrative is a lie [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.7]
dominance_rules.trigger: a why-line is drafted for card, weakness or plan
dominance_rules.action: state the cause that actually operates, even when it is mundane, and verify it with the faithfulness check

dominance_rules.rule: A bounded analogy dominates an unbounded one; a plain example dominates a leaky analogy
dominance_rules.rationale: an unbounded analogy imports false properties as surely as a false statement
dominance_rules.trigger: an analogy is proposed for a decode
dominance_rules.action: bound it to one property with a stated break-point or replace it with a plain example

dominance_rules.rule: The display-only truth dominates any decision narrative for a display-only number
dominance_rules.rationale: BKT/Elo/ItemElo/CalibrationBin drive no scheduling or selection as shipped [FACT-source: APP_RECON §6.9]
dominance_rules.trigger: copy is about to say a number changes what the learner sees
dominance_rules.action: state that the number is shown for insight and does not currently drive the plan

dominance_rules.rule: The registered term dominates any context-specific synonym for a named value
dominance_rules.rationale: synonym drift makes one number look like several different things
dominance_rules.trigger: new copy needs a noun for an already-registered value
dominance_rules.action: use the registered term and vary only the surrounding phrasing

dominance_rules.rule: The faithfulness check dominates publication speed
dominance_rules.rationale: shipping an unverified behavioral claim can mislead the learner about how the app works
dominance_rules.trigger: behavioral copy is ready to publish
dominance_rules.action: hold publication until the claim is cross-checked against code and the owning specialist

dominance_rules.rule: A promoted caveat dominates layer purity when a shallow layer risks a misread
dominance_rules.rationale: a caption whose caveat lives only deeper can be misread before the reader ever hovers
dominance_rules.trigger: a critical caveat sits below the layer where the value first appears
dominance_rules.action: promote the caveat to the shallowest layer that can carry it

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the reader model and vocabulary ceiling before writing any copy
anti_rework_rules.prevents: drafting engineer-voiced explanations that must all be rewritten for the actual learner

anti_rework_rules.rule: Adopt the honest-translation contract before decoding any term
anti_rework_rules.prevents: shipping decodes that overstate certainty and having to re-audit every tooltip later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Build the jargon inventory before authoring decodes
anti_rework_rules.prevents: missing a visible token or padding effort on internal fields the reader never sees

anti_rework_rules.rule: Author each definition once in the glossary and link to it everywhere
anti_rework_rules.prevents: inline-rewritten definitions drifting apart across UI, tooltip and guide

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix one term per concept in the registry before copy spreads
anti_rework_rules.prevents: synonym drift that has to be reconciled across many screens after the fact

anti_rework_rules.rule: Run the faithfulness check before a behavioral claim ships, not after
anti_rework_rules.prevents: publishing a phantom-decision or false-adaptivity claim that must be retracted

anti_rework_rules.rule: Pair each behavioral explanation with its logic dependency at authoring time
anti_rework_rules.prevents: silent staleness when the model changes and no review is triggered

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set a per-layer wording budget before writing tooltips
anti_rework_rules.prevents: crammed captions that must be re-split into the ladder later

iteration_protocol.trigger: a specialist changes a behavior the copy describes (selection, diagnosis, planning, mastery/Elo computation)
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the faithfulness check on the affected explanations and update them

iteration_protocol.trigger: a display-only number becomes decision-driving (e.g. mastery or Elo starts driving the queue)
iteration_protocol.action: rewrite its decode and why-surfaces to state the new decision role

iteration_protocol.trigger: the diagnosis confidence becomes an actual computed probability rather than a constant
iteration_protocol.action: revise the confidence decode from rule-strength framing to probability framing

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new UI surface exposes a new jargon token
iteration_protocol.action: add it to the inventory, author a decode and a glossary entry, and register its term

iteration_protocol.trigger: readers repeatedly misread a term or analogy that met the target
iteration_protocol.action: revise the reading level, the analogy bound, or the layer the caveat sits in

iteration_protocol.trigger: a named plain-language or help-system standard is adopted for source-verification
iteration_protocol.action: replace the ESTIMATE-tagged reading-level and technique guidance with the cited standard

iteration_protocol.trigger: a shipped surface is found to violate a no-go (constant-as-probability or phantom-decision)
iteration_protocol.action: correct the copy and add the case to the faithfulness-check checklist

priority_rationale: The frame, reader model and honest-translation contract come first because they decide, for every later sentence, who it is for and what truth it must preserve; the reading-level target, techniques, disclosure layering, information scent and analogy discipline come next as the form rules that make copy readable without falsifying it; the jargon inventory and the per-token decodes (FK/CC, mastery, Elo, retention, calibration, and the flagship confidence constant) then apply those rules to the app's actual visible tokens; the glossary, guide and term registry centralize the decodes into a reusable reference layer; and the why-surfaces, faithfulness check, maintenance sync and final verdict come last because they compose every explanation into an honest, behavior-faithful, kept-in-sync layer with an explicit no-go on calling a heuristic constant a probability or claiming a decision the app does not make.
